## Hard-to-vary report: Anselm's *Proslogion* 2–4, with Gaunilo and the reply

**1. The question, frozen.** The document does several jobs, but the one its title and opening make central is the argument of *Proslogion* 2–4: **does "something greater than which cannot be thought" prove that God exists in reality, and not merely in thought?** Range: one being, under that description, in the world. Asked: what produces what? — a backward-looking case, from a word we understand to a fact about the world. Gaunilo and Anselm's reply are the same question met with changes.

**2. The explanation in parts.** (A) The name/definition, "that than which a greater cannot be thought" — the Top. (B) Understanding the words puts the thing in the mind. (C) Existing in reality as well as in the mind is greater than existing in the mind alone. (D) So a Top that existed only in the mind would be one we could think greater — impossible, so it exists in reality too. (F) It cannot even be thought not to exist. (G) There are two ways a thing is "in the mind": the words, and the thing understood. (H) Whatever does not exist as a whole at some time or place can be thought away — parts can be broken up in the mind. (I) "Greater than all other things" is not "greater than which cannot be thought." (J) "I appeal to your faith and conscience." (K) The fool is stupid and foolish. (L) The painter's picture in his art.

**3. Part by part.**

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A the Top | Held | by Anselm's own swap (I): the same steps run for "greater than all other things" fail, and he says so. The wording is doing work. |
| B words ⇒ in the mind | Held if | held only by the job "the denier still has God in mind" — a job (G) itself concedes is doubtful. |
| C reality is greater than thought | Loose | Gaunilo denies it outright; its near neighbour ("existing in the mind is at least as good") does the job just as well. Asserted, never poked. |
| D the step to existence | Held if | held only by C, which is loose. |
| E "exists in thought and reality" | Idle | restates D; nothing is lost by cutting it. |
| F cannot be thought not to exist | Held | by the one change that had to be answered rather than absorbed: the lost island. The island can be thought away; the Top, on this clause, cannot. |
| G two senses of thinking | Held if | held by "why does the fool say it" — a job that shrinks quietly, since it makes his grasp words-only. |
| H parts, time, place | Held | the boldest testable part: it says *which* things are thinkable-away, and offers time and the world as cases. |
| I the two phrases | Held | it costs Anselm something (the island proof is abandoned) and so is not decoration. |
| J faith and conscience | Borrowed | rests on shared belief, not tested here. |
| K "stupid and foolish" | Idle | a label: no change tells it from any other insult. It is a second route to G's job. |
| L the painter | Held if | Gaunilo shows the picture in the painter's *art* is part of his mind; the analogy needs repair before it holds. |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.** *Flip:* Gaunilo supplies it — the same steps, aimed at an island, run just as smoothly. Once. Anselm's answer is the phrase swap (I), which is the only place the flip is met. *Answer in the starting points:* C smuggles "existence in reality is the greater thing" in as a ranking; Ch 4's "no one who understands can think God does not exist" is the conclusion under the name "understands". *Pull:* B ("the fool understands what he hears") against G ("the fool has only the words"). G gives way. Cost: the argument no longer speaks to the fool it was written against — Gaunilo's exact complaint. Second pull: J against the whole proof-to-reason programme. *Catch-all:* the definition absorbs any counterexample ("then it was not the Top"), but it comes with a gauge — H's test (parts, time, place) — so it is answerable. *Change list:* the island, the phrase swap, time and the world, the fool, the painter. What it leaves out is never stated: no change to the world would show the Top present or absent for anyone who has not already granted C. *Rivals:* Gaunilo's is the only one built properly, and it is answered. *Provenance:* A and C **asserted** (named, not tested); H and I **built** (worked out with the thing in view, committing to cases nobody had tried); G **built then patched**; J **borrowed**.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.** Two things. First, give C a poke: find one case where adding real existence makes a thing no greater — then say why God is not that case. Second, run H's test on a thing with no parts and no place or date — a number, or "twice two is four." If such a thing also cannot be thought away, the clause marks a kind of necessity, not God, and the proof shows only that *something* has it.

**6. What this does not show.** Loose is not false. C may be true and is simply not yet held by anything; passing the checks is not being right. This finds the loose bolts, and reports where Anselm's argument is genuinely bolted — the definition, the phrase-swap, the parts-and-places test — and where it is not.

**7. One next step.** Run the number case from §5 against H and report which way it falls.
